corrected_value.title: The Marley Hypothesis: Denial of racism reflects ignorance of history.

decisions.location: Results (lines 343-348); see also Abstract (lines 31-45), General Discussion (lines 600-625), and References (lines 845-849)
decisions.quote:
In the sections below, results for Study 1 are compared with those of the first or
“original” study on the Marley Hypothesis (Nelson et al., 2013). In subsequent discussion we

additionally highlight potential similarities and differences between the present findings and

those of the second study on the Marley Hypothesis (Bonam et al., 2018).
decisions.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists at the supplied context paths. Across two new studies (Study 1 N = 356; Study 2 N = 225) using the same Black History quiz, signal-detection d' scoring, and racism perception measures, this paper empirically retests the Marley Hypothesis mediation finding from Nelson, Adams, & Salter (2013) ('The Marley Hypothesis: Denial of racism reflects ignorance of history', Psychological Science, 24(2), 213-218, doi:10.1177/0956797612451466), directly comparing Study 1 and Study 2 means, effect sizes, confidence intervals, and Sobel/bootstrap mediation tests against Nelson et al.'s (2013) original N = 273 sample in the Results, Table 1, and Figure 1. The only supplied shipped row, input_row_index 2085 (10.1177/1948550617751583, Bonam, Nair Das, Coleman, & Salter, 2018, Social Psychological and Personality Science), is a separate subsequent study (target_index 1) conducted in a different sample (111 White and 43 Black students at a single racially diverse university) rather than an alternate report of Nelson et al. (2013) (199 White and 74 Black students from two HBCUs and a PWI). Nelson et al. (2013) is therefore a genuinely absent original target.
